5:10.t: After this there follows: And it shall come to pass in that day, when your hand has been lifted up over your foes, O Israel, and all your enemies have perished, I will kill your horses from your midst, that is, from the ruling part of your heart, the wanton impulses that rush forth like horses when their bonds are broken, and your chariots, in which you pleased yourself in your vices, and, joining sins to sins, were carried along as if triumphing in four-horse chariots.

5:11.t: And I will destroy the cities of your land: for you did not build the city which the rush of the river of God makes glad, and which is set on the mountains, and the heavenly Jerusalem, but the one which Cain had built. Hence they are called cities of the land, built with earthly works. And I will take away, he says, all your strongholds, namely riches and the pomp of the world, and the eloquence of rhetoricians and the little snares of dialecticians, in which you trusted as in strongholds.

5:12.t: And I will take away sorceries from your hands, by which either you yourself were deceived by others, or, being deceived, you deceived others; and those who speak, or pronounce, shall not be yours. Now the world is full of speakers and pronouncers; they speak what they do not know, they teach what they have not learned; they are teachers, though they were not pupils before. When, therefore, God teaches man knowledge, false presumptions will cease, and perverse doctrine will be removed.

5:13.t: And I will destroy your carved images and your pillars from your midst. Our carved images are those which were made by the speakers, or which we fashion for ourselves. Hence it is commanded in the law that we should not make a carved image for ourselves, and that we should not set up pillars in our land; and you shall no longer worship the works of your hands. Unhappy human condition, full of folly and error! It knows from what sense its doctrines were composed, it is not ignorant that the idol was feigned by itself, and yet in place of God it worships the works of its own hands, and man bows down, so that, deceived, he may deceive.

5:14.t: There is added, in the promise which is directed to the remnant, that is, the ὑπόλειμμα of Jacob: And I will cut down the groves from your midst, and I will destroy your cities, so that he may pull down and consume all the trees of the forests, and the groves which it was forbidden to plant in the temple of God, and the badly built cities which he had earlier called the cities of the land.

5:15.t: And after he has done this for the remnant of Jacob, then they will turn to the nations which the apostles grazed down like lambs grazing the grass. And because they were unwilling to receive the dew of speech, I will execute, he says, vengeance in anger and in fury on the nations, because they were unwilling to hear. Hence the prophet also says: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your anger. Let this be what we have discussed according to the Seventy translators, since it is the spiritual understanding, and we had to join the sense to the earlier sections.

6:1.t: Hear what the Lord says: Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, O mountains, the judgment of the Lord, and you strong foundations of the earth, for the judgment of the Lord will be decided with his people, and with Israel: LXX. Hear what the Lord has spoken: Arise, be judged before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, O mountains, the judgment of the Lord, and you valleys, foundations of the earth, for the judgment of the Lord is against his people, and with Israel it will be judged. 6:3.t: The third interruption of the Prophet is that, as he is stationed among people who exercise wickedness, he desires to be separated from their contamination. Many think that this refers to the Lord Jesus, because it is His alone not to fear judgment, since He conquers when He is judged. For He has a judgment from an unjust man, into which Christ willingly enters, as you have written: My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I saddened you? Moreover, when the father gives all judgment to him, not as if to an infirm person, but as if to a son, because he himself can undergo judgment? If they think that the judgment of the Father must be undergone by the Son, then the Father surely does not judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the son; […]

God, therefore, speaks to the people of Israel, and summons them to judgment, and grants them leave to dispute against him. My people, what have I done to you that I ought not to have done? Or how have I grieved you? although this is not found in the Hebrew. But a father grieves the son he has scourged, and the shepherd visits the iniquities of the sheep with the rod. In what have I been troublesome to you? Or, as is written more expressively in the Hebrew, with what toil have I oppressed you? […]

But we who long to contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, and truly have Abraham as our father, let us hear God, when we have sinned, disputing against us and reproving us by the greatness of his benefits. For we once served Pharaoh, and made mud and bricks for the Egyptian people, and he redeemed us who gave himself as a redemption for all, so that we who had been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemies and whom he gathered from the regions, might say: For his mercy is forever. He also sent before our face Moses, the spiritual law, and Aaron, the great priest, not bearing the typical ephod and the truth, but having on his forehead the seal of holiness which God the Father sealed. And he sent Miriam, the prophecy of the prophets; […]

6:5.t: You see the Lord is teaching you a lesson, challenging you to goodness by his own example, teaching you even when he reproves. When accusing the Jews, for instance, he says, "O my people, what have I done to you? Or wherein have I grieved you? Or wherein have I offended you? Answer me. Is it because I brought you out of the land of Egypt, and delivered you out of the house of bondage?" adding, "And I sent before your face Moses, Aaron and Miriam. O my people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised." You were indeed oppressed, an exile in foreign lands, laden with heavy burdens.

For the torrent of cords, or of thorns, Symmachus rendered the valley of thorns. Now there is a place near Livias, beyond the Dead Sea, six miles distant from Livias, where Israel once committed fornication with the Midianites. This place the prophet Micah mentions in the person of God, saying: My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam son of Beor answered, from Settim to Gilgal. For which there too the Seventy translated ἀπὸ τῶν σχοίνων, that is, from the cords to Gilgal.

My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I been troublesome to you, answer me, for I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and from the house of servants I freed you, and I sent before your face Moses, and Aaron and Miriam. My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, that you might know the justices of the Lord. LXX: My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you, or in what have I been troublesome to you? Answer me: for I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and from the house of bondage I redeemed you, and I sent before your face Moses, and Aaron and Miriam. […]

But if this seems little to you, remember that time when Balak king of Moab hired Balaam the diviner for a fee against you, and see how, against his own will, the soothsayer, wishing to curse you, blessed you; from Shittim to Gilgal, surveying with his eyes the whole army of Israel and changing places, as if I could not go with him as he went and pass over with him as he passed over; and this I did so that my mercies and justices might be known to you, for I love you so much that, while I am cursed daily by the mouth of blasphemers, I did not allow you to be cursed by the enemy. […]

For let us remember what he devised against us who wished to devour us and lick up our congregation: the true Balak, the devil. For Balak is interpreted ἐκλείχων, that is, licking up, king of the paternal water; since Moab, according to another etymology, is called paternal water. When, therefore, Balak was lying in wait for us, and lying in wait through his vain people, which is what Balaam is interpreted, God did not allow us to lie under his curses, but on the contrary there blessed us, compelled by the truth of the thing itself, the vain people of the nations, born of him who is in the skin — for Beor is interpreted in the skin — ever given over to the flesh and to the works of death; […]

6:6.t: Is everyone who is turning from sin to faith, turning from sinful practices (as if they were his mother) to life? I shall call in evidence one of the twelve prophets, who says, "Am I to make an offering of my firstborn son for my impiety? Should I offer the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?" Can the mother buy her way to God by giving up her firstborn? This must not be taken as an attack on the words "increase in numbers." Micah is naming, by using the word impiety, the first impulses after birth, which do not help us to knowledge of God. If anyone misuses this as a basis for saying that that birth is evil, he should also use it as a basis for saying that it is good, in that in it we come to know the truth. "Come back to a sober and upright life and stop sinning." […]

Then the word of the prophet, a little further on, suggests again the curtailing and abolition of the ancient ritual of the Law, speaking in the person of the people:

"6. Wherewithal shall I reach the Lord, and lay hold of my God most high?. Shall I reach him by whole burnt-offerings, by calves a year old? 7. Should I give my firstborn for my ungodliness, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"

And he makes this answer to them in the person of God:

"8. Has it not been told thee, O man, what is good? And what does the Lord require of thee, but to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk after thy God? […]
6:6.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 13

6:6.t: What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend the knee to God most high? Shall I offer him burnt offerings, and yearling calves? Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat he-goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul? LXX: With what shall I lay hold of the Lord? Shall I receive my God most high? Shall I lay hold of him with burnt offerings, with yearling calves? Will the Lord accept, with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of fat he-goats? If I give my firstborn for impiety: the fruits of my womb for the sin of my soul. God had summoned the people to judgment; […]

6:8.t: "But God,"[adulterers and fornicators say,] "is good and most kind." He is "merciful, compassionate and rich in mercy," which "he prefers to every sacrifice." "He desires not so much the death as the repentance of the sinner." He is "the Savior of all people, and especially of the faithful." Therefore the children of God must also be "merciful" and "peacemakers," "forgiving each other as Christ also forgave us," "not judging, lest we be judged." For to "his master a man stands or falls; who are you to judge the servant of another?" "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." Yet many such things as these are only said, not done, merely bandied about, unmanning rather than strengthening discipline, flattering God and pandering to themselves.

I will show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: surely to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God. LXX: It has been declared to you, man, what is good, or what the Lord requires of you, except that you do judgment, and love mercy, and be ready to walk with your God. Since you are in doubt, O people of Israel — or rather the whole human race, for I am by no means speaking to the people of the Jews, but my speech will run out generally to every man — how you can appease God for your sins, if you do not even have victims by which your impiety may be compensated, I will answer you what God requires; indeed, I have already shown it before in the law. […]

You ask what you should offer: offer yourself. For what else does the Lord seek of you but you? Because of all earthly creatures he has made nothing better than you, he seeks yourself from yourself, because you have lost yourself.

Here is a priest who serves at every hour with great fear while walking humbly with the Lord his God in accordance with the word of the prophet. Meanwhile another priest is hardly capable of having that much fear even when he is about to die and enter into the last judgment before his Lord. But the full expression of the priesthood is comprised of the combination of the teaching of truth with good works. This is in accord with blessed Luke's comment that in writing his Gospel he had composed a treatise concerning all the things that Jesus began both to do and to teach.

6:9.t: The voice of the Lord cries to the city, and there will be salvation for those who fear your name. LXX: The voice of the Lord will cry to the city, and he will save those who fear his name. In the Hebrew this is the beginning of the next section, but with the Seventy translators it is the end of the preceding one; and it has this sense: Your God asks nothing else of you, O man, except that you do judgment, and love mercy, and be ready to walk with your God. For the voice of the Lord is heard in his city, the Church, and resounds daily in the holy Scriptures, so that not only those who love mercy, but also those who are lower and still fear the name of the Lord, may be saved by his teaching and clemency. […]

Let us therefore return to the beginning of the section. And, discussing it first according to the letter, let us, with the help of your prayers, strive to attain the spiritual sense. Hear, ten tribes of Samaria, what the Lord solemnly declares to you: Still there is fire, that is, iniquity, in the house of the ungodly Omri, and the treasures of ungodliness persist in the royal house. Do you wish to hear, one by one, the evils of which your city is full? Learn: a scant measure that provokes the wrath of God, a deceitful balance and differing weights, and men who sell their wares by one weight and buy by another. And if indeed the poor were doing this, their want could have defended the crime by necessity. […]

Thus far we have set out what seemed right to us according to the Hebrew; now, returning to the translation of the LXX translators, let us discuss each point as best we can. The Samaritan tribe, which cut itself off from the people of God, is called to hear. And it is told: In vain you fashion idols, you put together golden calves with a craftsman's hand, and in imitation of Jerusalem you wish to build another metropolis; for who will be able to adorn the city? Can fire, which is kindled by the flaming darts of the devil, and the house of the wicked man, which according to its hardness and impenitent heart treasures up for itself wrath on the day of wrath, and of the revelation of the just judgment of God? […]

6:13.t: Hence the most merciful God does not strike them all at once, but strives little by little to admonish them through blows, saying: And I will begin to strike you with ruin on account of your sins; and the sense is: O city which the heretics wish to build, I will strike you so that you perish, not unto abolition, but in so far as you are a sinner.

When your princes were doing this, I did not wish to overthrow you at once, but little by little I began to strike you and to warn you with various blows. I sent famine upon you, I sent thirst, I sent diseases, and devastation by the enemy round about; the crop did not bring forth grain, the pressed olive did not yield oil, barren vintages denied the wine. Against the iniquities, and the deceitful measures, and the fraudulent weights, I brought these punishments.

6:14.t: There follows: You shall eat, and not be satisfied. For they read and do not understand; and feeding on the words of the Scriptures, they suffer a want of truth. And I will cast out, he says, you; and you shall lay hold, and shall not save; and whoever shall be saved shall be handed over to the sword. I will abandon you, he says, to your own judgment; and after you have sought many things and found nothing, understanding your error, you will see that you cannot be saved by all your doctrines. But whoever think themselves satisfied, and have not been cast out from themselves, nor have grasped the truth, will be handed over to the sword, and will be instructed by punishments.

6:15.t: You shall sow, therefore, O tribe, and O most wicked city, which the heretics build with fire, and iniquity, and insults, and a deceitful balance, and a fraudulent bag; you shall sow, and not reap; you shall press the olive, and not be anointed with oil; and the grapes, and not drink wine. Indeed it profits you, once your error is recognized, that you may not have disciples, that you may not anoint your head with the oil of sinners, that you may not make drunk with the wine of Sodom those who drink it.

6:16.t:
Hear, O tribes, and who will approve it?

Still there is fire in the house of the ungodly, treasures of ungodliness, and a scant measure full of wrath. Shall I justify an ungodly balance and the deceitful weights of the bag? By which her rich men were filled with iniquity, and those who dwell in her spoke lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. And I therefore have begun to strike you with ruin for your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied, and your humiliation is in the midst of you; and you shall lay hold and shall not save; and those whom you save I will give to the sword. You shall sow and not reap, you shall tread the olive and not be anointed with oil, and the must, and not drink wine. And you have kept the precepts of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab; […]

But because you kept all the ceremonies of idolatry which Omri, the ungodly king, had established, and observed every work of the house of Ahab and Jezebel in place of my law, I was driven by your crime to give you and your inhabitants up to hissing, and that you should bear the reproach of my people, while, taken captive by the Assyrians, you are conquered as if you were the people of God, and on your account my name is blasphemed among the nations. It should be noted in the present passage that where we read: And you shall bear the reproach of my people, or, as the LXX translated: You shall receive the reproaches of the peoples, Ammi is written in the Hebrew for 'of my people'. […]

And the statutes of my people, or of Omri, shall be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab, of those who stood forth as patriarchs and princes in the heresies. These we can refer either to the contrary powers or to the heresiarchs, such as were Marcion and Basilides, and recently Arius and Eunomius. And you walked in their wills, namely those of Omri and Ahab. And he says well, in their wills. For the teaching of wicked masters is not the teaching of God, but the inventions of their heart. And I will hand you over to ruin, so that you perish in so far as you are heretical. And your inhabitants to hissing, either so that you may follow the hissing of the good shepherd, according to Zechariah, who says: I will hiss for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them. […]

7:1.t: The unjust are scattered like chaff, while the just are like wheat. Finally, listen to the words of the Lord to Peter: Behold, Satan has desired to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. Those who are scattered like chaff will fail; but not the one who is like that grain which fell and rose again, enriched by the abundant yield of many fruits. Therefore the Prophet says: Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering straw in the harvest! Therefore, straw that is quickly burned is compared to impiety and to dust. Therefore, after he said: They will be like chaff carried away by the wind, he added the verse immediately saying: Or like the dust that the wind snatches away. […]

Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers the clusters of the vintage in autumn. There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs. The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright one among men. All lie in wait for blood, a man hunts his brother to death. The evil of their hands they call good; the prince demands, and the judge is for requiting, and the great man has spoken the desire of his soul, and they have troubled it. He who is best among them is like a brier, and he who is upright like a thorn from the hedge. LXX: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like clusters in the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat the first-ripe; which my soul has suffered. […]

Moreover, according to the Seventy, who disagree in certain points and at the end of the section translated altogether differently, the sense seems to me to be of this kind. The prophetic word, or the apostolic, laments over the human race in general, that the word has cast the seed of doctrines in vain, and that, instead of crops and grain, the late reaper has found scarcely empty stubble and hollow stalks, and has not been able to find even small clusters in the vineyard, and the rest up to the end of the section. For if he is blessed who speaks into the ears of one who listens, and the ear of the hearer is the desire of the wise man, and an understanding hearer is the joy of the speaker, on the contrary a bad pupil is the teacher's grief; […]

7:2.t: Cain and Abel followed in the generation of humankind, and Cain was the first murderer. Afterwards a deluge engulfed the earth because of exceeding wickedness of humanity. Fire came down from heaven upon the people of Sodom because of their corruption. Subsequently God chose out Israel, but even Israel became perverse and the chosen race was wounded. For, while Moses stood on the mountain before God, the people worshiped a calf in place of God. In the days of their lawgiver Moses, who said, "You shall not commit adultery," a man dared to enter a brothel and be wanton. […]

The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright one among men; everywhere ambushes, everywhere fraud, innocent blood is shed, for avarice and lust brotherhood is disregarded; and they not only do evil things but also defend them, and, exchanging the names, they say that what is evil is good. The princes themselves do not receive gifts from those who offer them, but compel their subjects to give, and demand them. And the judge is for requiting, judging another in the same way as he himself is judged by another, so that they may grant one another's crimes mutual favor and defend themselves in another's crime. Whoever is great and, as it were, most learned in the law speaks not God's will but his own. […]

The one returning has perished from the land, either because the Antichrist kills the saints, or because all fall away at the greatness of the stumbling-blocks. And there is none among men to correct; all are judged in blood, not in light and small sins, but in the greatest and in those that concern blood. Not neighborliness, not friendship, not kinship will hold back the crime; all will raise their hands to evil, so that even he who has not been able to do evil nevertheless sins by his will while he prepares his hands. The prince himself asks, and the judge speaks peaceful words; for he receives gifts, the desire of his soul. […]

7:4.t: For he who is best among them is like a brier, pricking and holding fast, wounding whoever comes near it and seizing him with a hooked tooth; and he who has been found upright is like a thorn from the hedge, so that pain is found where help was thought to be. This according to the Hebrew.

These the Lord threatens, saying: And I will take away their goods, which they think goods, which seem goods to them. But in the truth of the matter those things will never be called goods which both despoil the giver and kill the receiver; although it is not so much a threat as a blessing to take away evils from them, and for the Lord himself and the divine word to enter into their consciences and, like a moth, to devour whatever is perverse, and to lay waste their plunder and their evil thoughts, and to walk upon the norm and rule of truth, drawing back to what is right those very men who were led by depraved opinions; […]

The day of your watching, your visitation, comes; now shall be their devastation.

Do not believe a friend, and do not trust in a leader. From her who sleeps in your bosom guard the bars of your mouth, for the son does insult to the father, and the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are his own household. But I will look to the Lord, I will wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me. LXX: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come, now shall be their weeping; do not believe in friends, nor hope in leaders. From her who lies with you, beware lest you believe her, for the son does insult to the father, and the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; […]

There follows the exposition of the Seventy, who said: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come, that is, the punishments that are to be inflicted for crimes. To me, he says, belongs vengeance, and I will repay, says the Lord. And in another place: The days of your retribution have come. For the Lord executes vengeance for those who cry out to him day and night and say: How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Therefore the vengeances have come, and now shall be their weeping, that is, the weeping of the vengeances, so that those who laughed before may lament, and, as soon as they go out of the world, may endure torments, such as that rich man, once clad in purple and abounding in delights, endures in hell, where there is […]

Now we must discuss it according to the earlier interpretation, in which we spoke of the heretics: Hear, O tribe, and who has adorned the city? Is it fire and the house of the wicked? And again, of the Church: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest. And once more: Woe is me, O soul, the reverent man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men to correct. And thereafter: The prince asks, and the judge has spoken peaceful words, by the desire of his soul. Hence a double curse follows: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come; now shall be their lamentation, and let us say that it is written of the heretics: Do not believe in friends, O simple peoples, and in depraved leaders who promise that they are friends and princes of the heresies; […]

7:5.t: Therefore believe none of the voices of the prophets, and do not lend your ear to the deceiving flattery of the diviners, for if among dear names and the affection of kinship faith is rare, how much more so among those who, flattering you, lie for their own booty, and, as for sick men, prescribe not what is useful, but what is delightful and pleasing. Do not believe a friend; for indeed Ahithophel rose up against David, and the true Ahithophel, Judas, against Christ. And do not trust in a leader, as the men of Shechem trusted in Abimelech. For they themselves made him king, and were oppressed by him. From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the bars of your mouth, lest you suffer what Samson suffered from Delilah.

Therefore do not believe friends, for every friend supplants with supplanting, and he who is a friend for the sake of something is not so much the friend of him whom he pretends to love, for a friend takes his name from love, as of the thing that he loves. A certain man, asked what a friend was, replied: Another self. But if the example of the Pythagoreans is set against us, who gave themselves to the tyrant as sureties for one another, we say that the sentence was pronounced by God not generally against all friends and the affections of love, nor against every time, but concerning that time of which the Apostle says: In the last days perilous times will come: for men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, disdainful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, […]

Thus far it is commanded that we should not readily believe friends, leaders, wives. And a reason is given that does not quite answer to the proposition; for he says: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises against the mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household. For what has it to do with a friend, a leader, a wife, if son and daughter and daughter-in-law rise up against father and mother and mother-in-law? It seems to me, therefore, that it can be joined with what precedes in this way. […]

Before all things however we ought most carefully to observe the Evangelic precept, which tells us to enter into our chamber and shut the door and pray to our Father, which may be fulfilled by us as follows: We pray within our chamber, when removing our hearts inwardly from the din of all thoughts and anxieties, we disclose our prayers in secret and in closest intercourse to the Lord. We pray with closed doors when with closed lips and complete silence we pray to the searcher not of words but of hearts. We pray in secret when from the heart and fervent mind we disclose our petitions to God alone, so that no hostile powers are even able to discover the character of our petition. […]
7:5.s: The First Conference of Abbot Isaac, Chapter 35

7:5.t: A threefold war is threatening us: domestic, civil, and military. The first is with the flesh, which has many troops. This servant-maid is ever-willing to give access, as did Eve. Hence, Against her who lies in your bosom guard the portals of your mouth.

7:6.t: For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies are those of his household. This passage is written in nearly the same words in the prophet Micah. And note, wherever a testimony is set down from the Old Testament, whether the sense alone agrees or the wording as well.

For the son does insult to the father; Absalom, namely, to David: he defiled not only the kingdom but also the concubines of his father by incestuous intercourse. The daughter rises up against her mother: although for the present we find no testimony of this in the holy Scriptures, there are so many examples of it in daily life that we ought rather to mourn that they are so many than to search for them. The daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, as the wife of Esau rose up against Rebekah. A man's enemies are the men of his own household. Here I do not seek examples, since there are too many of them for us to need testimonies.

For the son who was born of God, neglecting his Creator, blasphemes him by whom he was made, as Scripture says: Has not one God created you? Is not one the father of all of you? And the soul despises the heavenly Jerusalem, and scorns her mother the Church, and whoever despises her shall die the death. And the daughter-in-law rises up against her mother-in-law: this seems difficult to understand according to tropology; but whoever has read the Song of Songs, and has understood the bridegroom of the soul to be the word of God, and has believed the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which was published and which we lately translated, in which it is said in the person of the Savior: Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by one of my hairs, will not hesitate to say that the word […]

7:7.t: Since, then, these things are so, do not believe, Samaria and Jerusalem, the false prophets. But I, says the prophet, will look to the Lord; I will exult in God my Savior, or my Jesus, and my God will hear me.

These things having thus been set forth, if indeed we have been able to reach the sense of the Scriptures, the holy man, understanding that love has grown cold, and that at the consummation of the world men are not lovers of God but lovers of themselves, while others believe in friends and leaders and wives, and son and daughter and daughter-in-law rise up against father and mother and mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household, himself believes in the Lord, and all his contemplation is in his God; […]

7:8.t: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; for though I have fallen, I will rise again. The ruin of weakness is not severe, if there is also not a desire to not rise from it. Have the will to rise, there is someone present who will make you rise.
7:8.s: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

7:8.t: Now let us come to the spiritual understanding, and, with the Holy Spirit himself expounding in what sense these things were written, let us toil even in the most difficult places. It seems to me that every soul, a Jerusalem in which the temple of the Lord was built, and the vision of peace, and the knowledge of the Scriptures, and which was afterwards overcome by sins, led into captivity and handed over to torments, speaks against Babylon, that is, the confusion of this world, and against the opposing power that presides over this world: Do not insult me, my enemy, because I have fallen, and I shall rise again; The Lord indeed lifts up those who are dashed down, and he speaks through the prophet: Shall he who falls not rise again? […]

Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise; when I sit in darkness: the Lord is my light. I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment for me; he will bring me out into the light, and I shall see his justice, and my enemy will look on, and she will be covered with confusion, who says to me: Where is the Lord your God? My eyes will look upon her; now she shall be trodden down, like the mud of the streets, the day for your walls to be built. On that day the law shall be far off; on that day they will come even to you from Asshur, and as far as the fortified cities, and from the fortified cities as far as the river, and to sea from sea, and to mountain from mountain. […]

A different thing is death of the soul and complete destruction and total abandonment. This is known thereby that, although one falls, he does not forget the love of his Father; and although he is loaded with trespasses of every kind, his zeal for the service of good is not held back, nor does he desist from his course, nor abhor to stand in struggle against these things anew and with the same chance of being vanquished, nor cease from demolishing every day his building and beginning a [new] foundation.

And the word of the prophet is in his mouth: Till the hour of my departure from this world, rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me. And he will not cease to struggle till death. […]

7:9.t: But there is no small danger of the mind falling into the error of supposing that every illness needs the aid of medicine. For not all illnesses come naturally, or from errors of diet or any other bodily causes, for which we see that the medical art is sometimes useful. For often illnesses are scourges of sins, sent to convert us. “For whom the Lord loveth, he chasteneth.” And “For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep. For if we discerned ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.” […]

There follows: I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, and executes judgment for me, and brings me out into the light; and I shall see his justice. All correction for the present seems to be a matter not of joy but of sorrow, but afterwards it will yield the peaceful fruit of justice to those who have been trained by it. The soul, therefore, perceiving that it has sinned, and has the wounds of sins, and lives in dead flesh, and needs cautery, says steadfastly to the physician: Burn my flesh, cut away the wounds, bind up all the humors and the noxious ῥεῦμα (flux) with a harsh draught of hellebore. It was my fault that I was wounded; let it be my pain that I endure so many torments, and afterwards receive health. […]

7:10.t: But when the Lord has brought us out into the light, and we have seen his justice, then our enemy Babylon will see, and will be covered with confusion, she who formerly said to us: Where is your God, thinking that Jerusalem after her wounds could not be healed. And our eyes will look upon her, and she will be trodden down like the mud of the streets.

7:11.t: For as to what is said according to the Seventy, The day of the daubing of brick, your blotting out, let us understand that it is said not to Jerusalem, as we expounded according to the Hebrew, but still to Babylon: that she too is to be blotted out, and trodden down like brick. And that day will thrust back the ordinances: not the ordinances of God, but those ordinances which, O Babylon, you had commanded to be observed against the law of God.

Thus far Jerusalem has spoken, or the prophet in the person of the people; now God is brought in answering Jerusalem: O Jerusalem, the days have come for your walls to be built, which had been destroyed by the Babylonian when he laid you waste. On that day the law shall be far off, or the precept and command, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated, saying ἐπιταγὴν καὶ πρόσταγμα; and the sense is: You will by no means lie subject to the rule of the Babylonians; on that day on which your walls will be built, they will come to you from Asshur, and from the fortified cities; from the fortified cities, I say, as far as the Jordan, across which the people also passed before, and from the Red Sea; […]

And since every end of punishments is the beginning of good things, and pain advances toward health, bricks will be made from her mud, and her daubing will be the shaping of bricks. And on that day she will cast off her old errors, and her cities, which had been badly fortified, will come into enclosure, or into division, and will be divided by the Assyrians; from Tyre too, which is interpreted συνοχὴ, that is, distress, other powers will rise up, and there will be sedition even as far as those who delight in the flux of this age and beget lusts in men. And from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain, wars will rise up against one another, so that bitterness fights against bitterness, and a loftiness that exalts itself and is to be humbled contends against another height; […]

7:12.t: And your cities will come into enclosure, or into division, with the Assyrians attacking you — since indeed Babylon was a city of the Chaldeans, not of the Assyrians —. And your fortified cities will be for the division of a hostile army, from Tyre as far as the river Tigris, by which you are encircled, and from the Great Sea as far as the Red Sea, which, on the flank, for those traveling to India, touches your regions. And from mountain to mountain; namely, from the mountains of Judea as far as the mountains of Media and of the Persians, all Mesopotamia and the whole region which is now held by you in the middle will be subjugated to the rule of your adversaries. And the land shall become a desolation because of the most wicked fruits of your pursuits. […]

7:14.t: Shepherd your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest in the midst of Carmel; they shall feed on Bashan and Gilead according to the days of old, according to the days of your going out from the land of Egypt; I will show him wonders. The nations shall see, and shall be confounded at all their strength. They shall put their hands upon their mouth; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the dust like serpents, like the creeping things of the earth; they shall be troubled out of their dwellings. They shall dread the Lord our God, and they shall fear you. LXX: Shepherd your people with your rod, the sheep of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest; […]

7:15.t: The divine word also promises that he will show wonders to his people and to the sheep of his inheritance: Then, he says, the nations shall see, and shall be confounded in all their strength, because they had once laid waste and prevailed against the people of God; and their confusion will bring them progress, when they have understood their own evils. For they will put their hands upon their mouth, and their evil works will take from them all freedom of speaking. But just as the hands of the impious nations close their mouths, so the hands of the just will open their mouths, as they receive from good work the faculty of speaking with God. Their ears too will grow deaf, because malice has not only blinded the gaze of the eyes but has also made the ears grow deaf; […]

Hear what is even more wonderful, that the hidden and veiled mysteries of the ancient books are in some degree revealed by the ancient books. For Micah the prophet speaketh thus. “According to the days of thy coming out of Egypt will I show unto him marvellous things, etc.…In this Psalm, therefore, although the wonderful spirit of prophecy doth look into the future, yet it seemeth, as it were, to be merely detailing to the past. “Judah,” he saith, “was His sanctuary: the sea saw that and fled:” “was,” “saw,” and “fled,” are words of the past tense; […]

7:16.t: And these things will happen so that the nations may see, and be confounded in all their evil strength, and put their hands upon their mouth, and grow deaf in their ears, and lick the earth like serpents that drag the ground, so that first they may be shut in, and, once shut in, be troubled, then, terrified, be astonished before the Lord God of the saints, and at last they too may fear him. This is according to the LXX. Moreover, since our edition, at least in the present passage, does not differ much from them, let us consider that what has been said on theirs has been said on this also.

7:17.t: After such great evils it is said of them that they will lick the ground like serpents that drag the earth, walking on their belly and eating earth all the days of their life. And doing the works of the flesh, that is, earthly works, and dragging with them, up to the day of the vengeance and visitation of the Lord, not dust, not small traces of earth, but the whole ground. And when they have done this, and have come to the judgment of God, and have been shut in and troubled, they will be troubled and shut in for as long as the earth which they had dragged like serpents remains in them. But when that has failed, they will be astonished and will marvel, not at the Lord their God — for they will not yet deserve that he be called the Lord their God —, but at the Lord our God. […]

7:18.t:
Wherefore let us not listen to him when we are in any of the troubles of this world, be it bodily pain, or the loss of our children, or of other necessaries, let us not listen to his words, Where is the Lord thy God? It is under severe pain that his temptations are to be feared, it is then that he seeks to turn the sick soul astray.

Wherefore the soul which has not listened to his allurements, seeing afterwards the wonderful works of God, seeing herself in heaven, and the devil creeping upon the earth, will congratulate herself saying, Who is a God like unto Thee, that pardoneth iniquity and passeth by transgression?

Who is a God like you? You who take away iniquity, and pass over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance. He will not send his fury any more, because he is one who wills mercy. He will return and have mercy on us; he will put away our iniquities, and will cast all our sins into the depth of the sea. You will give truth in Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from the days of old. LXX: Who, O God, is like you? Taking away iniquities, and passing over injustices for those who are left of your inheritance? He did not hold his anger as a testimony, because he is one who wills mercies. He will return, and will have mercy on us, he will sink our sins; and all our sins shall be cast into the depth of the sea. […]

Moreover, where we translated, He will not send his fury any more, for "any more" Symmachus rendered "forever", Theodotion "to the end", the Seventy and the Fifth Edition "as a testimony", for which laed is set in the Hebrew; and it can be understood as "any more" as well as "forever" and "testimony".

Moreover, what follows, For those who are left of his inheritance, he did not hold his anger as a testimony, has this sense: if he spared the nations, which would not believe his law, and would not impute their iniquities to those who were left over and left remaining of the people, nor brought his anger as a testimony of their just punishment, what will he do with his own flock, which feeds in the midst of Carmel, and in Bashan, and in Gilead? For he is one who wills mercy, and returning he will have mercy on us; and our heavy sins, and the iniquities that sit upon the talent of lead, he himself will carry, and will sink in the sea, and will not let them appear.

I too will say at the end of the volume, sealing the labor of my little work with an invocation of the Lord: God, who is like you? Take away the iniquity of your servant; pass over the sin of the remnant of my soul; do not send your fury upon me, nor rebuke me in your anger, since you are merciful, and your mercies are many. Return, and have mercy on me; hurl down my iniquities, and cast them into the depth of the sea, so that the saltiness and bitterness of vices may perish in a false region. Give the truth that you promised to your friend Jacob, and the mercy that you promised to your friend Abraham, and free my soul from the persecutors of your prophets, Ahab and Jezebel, as you swore to my fathers in the days of old, saying: As I live, says the Lord. […]

7:19.t: We ought therefore to strip ourselves and give to him who is naked. One has God, another has him not at all—that contrary power, namely. And just as it is written that "we should cast our sins into the depth of the sea", so we ought to throw off from ourselves our vices and sins and cast them upon him who was for us the cause of them. "And he who has food", he says, "let him do likewise". He who has food, let him give to him who has none, so that he may bestow upon him not only clothing, but also that which he may eat.
7:19.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 23

7:19.t: He will turn again and have compassion upon us; he will tread our iniquities under foot, and all our sins shall be cast into the depths of the sea. He will perform the truth to Jacob and the mercy to Abraham, as he hath sworn unto our fathers from the days of old.

7:20.t: He will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, so that to the people that is a supplanter, and new, and always set in wrestling, he may render his truth in Christ, and to the multitude of the nations — for Abraham is called the father of many nations — he may grant mercy, as he swore to those who were the fathers of our faith according to the days of old, that out of the whole multitude of men he would save some in truth, others in mercy.
